hints: Think about the colour of aqueous bromine to start with and what happens to that colour when bromine is used up in a reaction.
Remember that bromination of phenylamine gives a heavily brominated organic solid that is insoluble in water, so consider what phase you would see.
walkthrough:
Picture the starting reagent**
Aqueous bromine, often called bromine water, is a familiar orange to brown solution. Whenever bromine reacts and is consumed, that colour disappears. So keep your eye on the colour change first.

Link to the very reactive ring in phenylamine**
In $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2$, the lone pair on nitrogen is delocalised into the benzene ring. That makes the ring very electron rich and very easily attacked by the electrophile $\text{Br}_2$, even without a catalyst. So bromine is rapidly used up and its colour is lost to give colourless $\text{Br}^-$ and $\text{HBr}$ in solution.

Spot the insoluble product**
The organic product is 2,4,6-tribromophenylamine, which is a large non-polar molecule that is insoluble in water. It therefore separates out as a white solid, so you see a white precipitate forming as the bromine colour fades.

Final answer: Aqueous bromine is decolourised from orange / brown to colourless.
A white precipitate is formed.

hints: Compare $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2$ with $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2$ and ask whether ethylamine has a benzene ring that can undergo bromination.
walkthrough:
Check what ethylamine can and cannot do**
$\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2$ is an aliphatic amine. It has no benzene ring, so it cannot undergo electrophilic substitution on a ring like phenylamine does. There is no activated aromatic system for $\text{Br}_2$ to attack.

Conclude the observation**
Because no bromination reaction occurs, the bromine stays as $\text{Br}_2(aq)$. You will simply see the orange / brown solution remain with no decolourisation and no white precipitate. That contrast is exactly why this test distinguishes the two amines.
Final answer: No change / no reaction. The orange / brown colour of aqueous bromine remains and no precipitate forms.

hints: Recall that the $\text{-NH}_2$ group strongly activates the benzene ring and directs incoming electrophiles to the 2, 4 and 6 positions, and excess bromine gives maximum substitution.
walkthrough:
Use the directing power of the amino group**
Think of $\text{-NH}_2$ as a powerful activator. Its lone pair pumps electron density into the ring, especially at the 2, 4 and 6 positions relative to nitrogen (the two ortho positions and the para position). With excess aqueous bromine, all three of these positions react.

Draw the trisubstituted product**
Keep the $\text{NH}_2$ group at the top of the ring as position 1. Then place a $\text{Br}$ atom at each ortho position (left and right next to $\text{NH}_2$) and one $\text{Br}$ atom at the para position (directly opposite $\text{NH}_2$). That gives a symmetrical $\text{C}_6\text{H}_2\text{Br}_3\text{NH}_2$ structure with three $\text{C-Br}$ bonds on the ring.
Final answer: Benzene ring with $\text{NH}_2$ at position 1 and $\text{Br}$ at positions 2, 4 and 6 (2,4,6-tribromophenylamine): $\text{C}_6\text{H}_2\text{Br}_3\text{NH}_2$.

hints: Name the parent as phenylamine (or aniline) and number the three bromo substituents from the $\text{NH}_2$ carbon as position 1.
walkthrough:
Build the systematic name**
Start with the parent amine. Phenylamine and aniline are two accepted names for $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2$. The Cambridge mark scheme uses the phenylamine root here.

Add the locants for three bromines**
Number the ring so the carbon bearing $\text{NH}_2$ is carbon 1. The bromines sit at the two ortho carbons, 2 and 6, and the para carbon, 4. Join them together as 2,4,6-tribromo in front of phenylamine to give 2,4,6-tribromophenylamine.
